caption.p: (a) Orientation tuning curves corresponding to the V1 encoding matrix (Wzx\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{zx}$\end{document}). Each row represents the tuning curve of a V1 neuron. The weight matrix itself has positive and negative synaptic weights like standard models of orientation-selective receptive fields. (b) The recurrent connectivity matrix for V1 (W11\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{11}$\end{document}). The V2 recurrent connectivity matrix W22\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{22}$\end{document} has a similar structure. (c) The feedback connectivity matrix from V2 to V1 (W12\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{12}$\end{document}). The corresponding feedforward matrix from V1 to V2, (W21\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{21}$\end{document}), is its transpose. Since W21\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{21}$\end{document} is symmetric, the feedforward and feedback matrices are identical (W12=W21\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{12}=\mathbf{W}_{21}$\end{document}).

sec.p: Both the V1 and V2 neurons follow the normalization equation exactly when β\begin{document}$\beta$\end{document} and γ\begin{document}$\gamma$\end{document} are set to unity (i.e. when there is identical feedback to principal neurons [y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}] and inhibitory modulator [a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}] neurons) and W11\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{11}$\end{document} is the identity matrix (i.e. each neuron recurrently amplifies itself), but the circuit closely approximates normalization for a wide range of parameters. For V1 neurons, normalization is expressed as:(2)y1+=⌊z1⌋2σ2+N1⌊z1⌋2,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{y}_{1}^{+} = \frac{\lfloor \mathbf{z}_{1} \rfloor^{2}}{\sigma^{2} + \mathbf{N}_{1}\lfloor \mathbf{z}_{1} \rfloor^{2}}, $$\end{document}

and likewise for V2(3)y2+=⌊z2⌋2σ2+N2⌊z2⌋2,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{y}_{2}^{+} = \frac{\lfloor \mathbf{z}_{2} \rfloor^{2}}{\sigma^{2} + \mathbf{N}_{2}\lfloor \mathbf{z}_{2} \rfloor^{2}}, $$\end{document}

where z2=W21y1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{z}_{2}=\mathbf{W}_{21}\mathbf{y}_{1}^{+}$\end{document} is the drive from V1 to V2, σ\begin{document}$\sigma$\end{document} is the semi-saturation constant. Normalization is achieved dynamically via recurrent amplification (amplifying weak inputs but not strong inputs) with the three modulatory neurons, u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document}, a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}, and q1\begin{document}$\mathbf{q}_{1}$\end{document} whose dynamics are governed by Equation 1b, Equation 1c, and Equation 1d, respectively. The equations for modulatory neurons are derived by substituting the normalization equation (Equation 2) in the equation for the principal neurons (Equation 1a) (see Appendix 1 for derivation). An increase in the activity of principal neurons (y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}) leads to enhanced activation in u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document} and q1\begin{document}$\mathbf{q}_{1}$\end{document}. This, in turn, drives a net increase of activity in modulatory neurons (a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}). The elevated a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document} activity subsequently exerts an inhibitory effect on y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}, thereby implementing normalization by the recurrent interactions between the neural populations (see Appendix 1 for derivation).

The parameter γ1\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}$\end{document} modulates the feedback gain to the principal neuron population (y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}). This determines the relative feedback to the principal neurons (y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}) compared to the inhibitory modulator neurons (a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}). As a rule of thumb, γ1\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}$\end{document}<1 indicates greater feedback inhibition, γ1\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}$\end{document} = 1 denotes a balance between feedback excitation and inhibition, and γ1\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}$\end{document}>1 signifies more feedback excitation. For simplicity, we have set the feedback to the inhibitory neurons (a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}) at a fixed value of 0.50 (hence, the factor of 12\begin{document}$\frac{1}{2}$\end{document} in Equation 1c and Equation 1a, see Appendix 1). Similarly, the parameter β1\begin{document}$\beta_{1}$\end{document} modulates the relative input gain to the principal neuron population (y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}) compared to the modulatory excitatory neuron population (u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document}). For simplicity, we set the input gain to the modulatory neurons (u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document}) to 0.50 (hence, the factor of 12\begin{document}$\frac{1}{2}$\end{document} in Equation 1a and Equation 1b). Note that when β1\begin{document}$\beta_{1}$\end{document} and γ1\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}$\end{document} are both set to unity and the recurrent matrix is identity, the network achieves excitatory-inhibitory balance exactly, and the normalization (Equation 2) is followed precisely.

We modeled each brain area using a ring model, where principal neurons are arranged in a circle to represent continuous features like stimulus orientation. The recurrent connectivity between these neurons is determined by the distance between them (Figure 7b). Each modeled area consists of 72 neurons for each of the four specified types (y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document},u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document},a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document},q1\begin{document}$\mathbf{q}_{1}$\end{document}). To simulate sensory input, a visual stimulus with a defined contrast and orientation is presented. The input drive is the product of the stimulus vector with the encoding matrix, whose rows are the tuning curves of the V1 principal neurons (Figure 7a). The tuning curves are modeled as raised cosine functions, each peaking at the neuron’s preferred orientation.

sec.title: Numerical computation of fixed points
sec.p: For all results reported here, the fixed point was computed numerically by integrating the deterministic dynamics to steady state. Starting from small uniform initial conditions, the dynamics were integrated with an adaptive Runge-Kutta scheme (RK45; relative and absolute tolerances of 10–10) over a window spanning several thousand times the slowest time constant. The steady state was accepted when every state variable changed by less than 10–6 between consecutive output samples, and the Jacobian at the fixed point was verified to have eigenvalues with negative real parts (i.e. a stable fixed point).

The numerically computed fixed points closely approximate Equation 2, to within 0.6% with the center-surround recurrent weight matrix (not the identity) and the feedback gain γ1\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}$\end{document} set to one. The deviation from the normalization fixed point increases as the feedback gain γ1\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}$\end{document} and the input gain β1\begin{document}$\beta_{1}$\end{document} deviate from 1.0.

sec.title: Power and coherence spectra
sec.p: The time evolution of neural population activity in V1 and V2 can be described by a general stochastic differential equation (SDE) with an additive noise term LdW\begin{document}$\mathbf{L}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}$\end{document}:(4)dx=f(x, u)dt+LdW,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathrm{d\textbf{x}}= \mathrm{\textbf{f(x, u)}d}t + \mathrm{\textbf{L}d\textbf{W}},$$\end{document}

where x∈Rn\begin{document}$\mathrm{\textbf{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$\end{document} is a vector representing the activity of neurons; f(x, u)∈Rn\begin{document}$\mathrm{\textbf{f(x, u)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$\end{document} represents the deterministic part of the dynamics explained above (Equation 1); dW\begin{document}$\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}$\end{document} is a vector of independent Gaussian increments with correlation matrix D (E[dW⋅dWT]\begin{document}$\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{T}}]$\end{document}), and L∈Rn×n\begin{document}$\mathbf{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$\end{document} is the dispersion matrix defining how noise enters the system. Given the fixed point of the dynamical system, we can linearize the system around the fixed point (x*):(5)dx=Jx∗(x−x∗)dt+LdW,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathrm{d\textbf{x}}= \mathrm{\textbf{J}_{\textbf{x}^*}(\textbf{x}- \textbf{x}^*)d}t + \mathrm{\textbf{L}d\textbf{W}},$$\end{document}

where Jx∗\begin{document}$\mathrm{\textbf{J}_{\textbf{x}^{*}}}$\end{document} is the Jacobian computed at the fixed point x∗\begin{document}$\mathrm{\textbf{x}^{*}}$\end{document}. This linearization leads to a wide-sense stationary Gaussian process, x(t)\begin{document}$\mathbf{x}(t)$\end{document}, whose power spectral density matrix, S(ω)∈Rn×n\begin{document}$\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$\end{document}, is given by Rawat and Martiniani, 2024b:(6)S(ω)=E[|x^(ω)|2]=(ıωI+J)−1LDLT(−ıωI+J)−T.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)=\mathbb{E}\left[|{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\omega)|^{2}\right]= (\imath\omega\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J})^{-1}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{L}^{ \mathsf{T}}(-\imath\omega\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J})^{-\mathsf{T}}.$$\end{document}

From S(ω)\begin{document}$\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)$\end{document}, we can directly compute the coherence, κij\begin{document}$\kappa_{ij}$\end{document}, between any two neurons i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} in the two areas:(7)κij=|Sij|2SiiSjj.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \kappa_{ij}= \frac{|\mathcal{S}_{ij}|^{2}}{\mathcal{S}_{ii}\mathcal{S}_{jj}}.$$\end{document}

The linearization was validated by direct numerical integration of the full nonlinear stochastic system, including all noise sources, with the Euler-Maruyama scheme (time step 10 µs; 100 independent trials of 16 s after a 1 s burn-in, at each contrast); power and cross-spectra were estimated from the simulated trajectories by Welch’s method (4 s segments, 50% overlap) and compared with Equations 6 and 7 (Appendix 1—figure 6; Appendix 1, ‘Numerical validation of the analytical spectra’). A quantitative comparison with experimental spectra, in which the model parameters are fitted, is described in Appendix 1 (‘Quantitative fit to experimental power and coherence spectra’) and shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

sec.title: Communication subspaces
sec.p: Here, we present the method used to characterize the communication subspaces between two subpopulations (source and target) of neurons (Semedo et al., 2019). These subpopulations may comprise distinct neurons in the same brain area or across different brain areas. The basic idea is to determine how well the fluctuations in responses of a target subpopulation can be predicted using a linear transform (a weighted sum) of the fluctuations in responses of the source subpopulation and to determine the dimensionality of this linear transform.

The fluctuations in the responses and their co-variability are fully determined by the correlation matrix at steady state when the strength of the noise is small. Therefore, the correlation matrix, denoted as C(0)\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}(0)$\end{document}, for the responses x(t)\begin{document}$\textbf{x}(t)$\end{document} can be computed by solving the Lyapunov equation:(8)JC(0)+C(0)JT=−LDLT.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{J}\mathbf{C}(0) + \mathbf{C}(0)\mathbf{J}^{\mathsf{T}}= -\mathbf{L}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{L}^{\mathsf{T}}.$$\end{document}

Once C(0)\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}(0)$\end{document} is obtained, we follow the method proposed by Semedo et al., 2019, to construct an analytical model of the communication subspace. To achieve this, we divide the mean-subtracted responses of the entire neuronal population, denoted as x, into two subsets: s (responses of the source neurons, e.g. in V1) and t (responses of the target neurons, e.g. in V2 or V1). We consider a linear model for predicting target responses using the source responses, t^=BTs\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{t}}=\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{s}$\end{document}, where the mean squared error (MSE) is given by:(9)ε=E[|t−BTs|2]=Tr(C2+BTC1B−2BTC3),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \varepsilon = \mathbb{E}[|\mathbf{t}- \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{s}|^{2}] = \text{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{2} + \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1}\mathbf{B}- 2\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{3}),$$\end{document}

where C1=E[ssT]\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{1}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{ss}^{\mathsf{T}}]$\end{document}, C2=E[ttT]\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{2}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{tt}^{\mathsf{T}}]$\end{document}, and C3=E[stT]\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{3}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{st}^{\mathsf{T}}]$\end{document}. These matrices can be directly obtained from C(0)\begin{document}$\textbf{C}(0)$\end{document}. To find the optimal readout matrix Bopt\begin{document}$\textbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}$\end{document}, we minimize ε\begin{document}$\varepsilon$\end{document} with respect to B\begin{document}$\mathbf{B}$\end{document}, leading to the ordinary least squares solution:(10)Bopt=C1−1C3\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \textbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}= \mathbf{C}_{1}^{-1}\mathbf{C}_{3}$$\end{document}

First, we define the covariance of the target activity predicted by the optimal model (note the ‘hats’), which we denote as C^2\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}$\end{document}:(11)C^2=E[t^t^T]=BoptTC1Bopt\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2} = \mathbb{E}[\hat{\mathbf{t}}\hat{\mathbf{t}}^{\mathsf{T}}] = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1} \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}$$\end{document}

By substituting the expression for Bopt\begin{document}$\textbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}$\end{document}, we arrive at a key relationship:(12)C^2=(C1−1C3)TC1(C1−1C3)=C3TC1−1C3\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2} = \left(\mathbf{C}_{1}^{-1}\mathbf{C}_{3} \right)^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1} \left(\mathbf{C}_{1}^{-1}\mathbf{C}_{3}\right) = \mathbf{C}_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1}^{-1}\mathbf{C}_{3}$$\end{document}

The principal dimensions of this predicted covariance matrix, C^2\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}$\end{document}, define the communication subspace. These are found by computing the eigen decomposition:(13)C^2=VΛVT\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2} = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}$$\end{document}

Here, the columns of the orthogonal matrix V\begin{document}$\mathbf{V}$\end{document} are the eigenvectors of C^2\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}$\end{document} and Λ\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$\end{document} is a diagonal matrix of the corresponding eigenvalues, sorted in descending order. The prediction performance for a reduced-rank approximation of dimension i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} is defined as: a rank-i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} approximation, BRRR\begin{document}$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{RRR}}$\end{document}, is constructed by projecting the optimal solution Bopt\begin{document}$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}$\end{document} onto the subspace spanned by the top i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} eigenvectors of C^2\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}$\end{document}.(14)BRRR(i)=BoptV(i)VT(i)=BoptPi\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{RRR}}(i) = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}\mathbf{V}(i) \mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}(i) =\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}\mathbf{P}_{i}$$\end{document}

where V(i)\begin{document}$\mathbf{V}(i)$\end{document} is a matrix containing first i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} columns of V\begin{document}$\mathbf{V}$\end{document}. Here, Pi=V(i)VT(i)\begin{document}$\mathbf{P}_{i}=\mathbf{V}(i)\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}(i)$\end{document} is the projection matrix. Note that Pi\begin{document}$\mathbf{P}_{i}$\end{document} is symmetric (PiT=Pi\begin{document}$\mathbf{P}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{P}_{i}$\end{document}) and idempotent (Pi2=Pi\begin{document}$\mathbf{P}_{i}^{2}=\mathbf{P}_{i}$\end{document}). We define the prediction performance as:(15) Performance(i)=1−εiε0,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{ Performance}(i)= 1- \frac{\varepsilon_{i}}{\varepsilon_{0}},$$\end{document}

where εi\begin{document}$\varepsilon_{i}$\end{document} is the MSE for the rank-i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} approximation(16)εi=Tr(C2+BRRRT(i)C1BRRR(i)−2BRRRT(i)C3).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \varepsilon_{i} = \text{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{2} + \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{RRR}}^{\mathsf{T}}(i)\mathbf{C}_{1}\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{RRR}}(i) - 2\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{RRR}}^{\mathsf{T}}(i)\mathbf{C}_{3}).$$\end{document}

ε0\begin{document}$\varepsilon_{0}$\end{document} is the MSE for the case where the readout matrix is a null matrix, corresponding to the total variance of the target population (ε0=Tr(C2)\begin{document}$\varepsilon_{0}=\mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{2})$\end{document}).

To simplify the expressions for εi\begin{document}$\varepsilon_{i}$\end{document}, we substitute BRRR(i)=BoptPi\begin{document}$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{RRR}}(i)=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}\mathbf{P}_{i}$\end{document} into the expression:(17)εi=Tr(C2)−Tr(2PiBoptTC3−PiBoptTC1BoptPi)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \varepsilon_{i} = \text{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{2}) - \text{Tr}\left(2 \mathbf{P}_{i} \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{3} - \mathbf{P}_{i} \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1}\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}\mathbf{P}_{i}\right) $$\end{document}

Now, we substitute BoptT=C3TC1−1\begin{document}$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{C}_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{ 1}^{-1}$\end{document} and recognize that the term BoptTC1Bopt\begin{document}$\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1}\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{opt}}$\end{document} is C^2\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}$\end{document}. Using the cyclic property of the trace (Tr(AB)=Tr(BA)\begin{document}$\text{Tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})=\text{Tr}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A})$\end{document}) and the idempotent property of the projection matrix (Pi2=Pi\begin{document}$\mathbf{P}_{i}^{2}=\mathbf{P}_{i}$\end{document}), we can simplify further:(18)εi=Tr(C2)−Tr(C^2Pi)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \varepsilon_{i} = \text{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{2}) - \text{Tr}(\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2} \mathbf{P}_{i})$$\end{document}

By applying the cyclic property and expanding Pi\begin{document}$\mathbf{P}_{i}$\end{document}, we can see that the second term is the sum of the top i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} eigenvalues (λj\begin{document}$\lambda_{j}$\end{document}) of C^2\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}$\end{document}.(19)Tr(C^2V(i)V(i)T)=Tr(V(i)TC^2V(i))=∑j=1iλj\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{Tr}(\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2} \mathbf{V}(i)\mathbf{V}(i)^{\mathsf{T}}) = \text{Tr}(\mathbf{V}(i)^{\mathsf{T}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2} \mathbf{V}(i)) = \sum_{j=1}^{i}\lambda_{j}$$\end{document}

Now the expression for prediction performance simplifies to:(20)Performance(i)=∑j=1iλjTr(C2),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{Performance}(i) = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{i}\lambda_{j}}{\text{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{2})},$$\end{document}

which can also be interpreted as:(21)Performance(i)=Explained variance (i dimensions)Total target variance.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{Performance}(i) = \frac{\text{Explained variance ($i$ dimensions)}}{\text{Total target variance}}.$$\end{document}

The maximum prediction performance (full-rank approximation) is given by:(22)Performance=Tr(C^2)Tr(C2)=Tr(C3TC1−1C3)Tr(C2)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{Performance}= \frac{\text{Tr}(\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2})}{\text{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{2})}= \frac{\text{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1}^{-1}\mathbf{C}_{3})}{\text{Tr}(\mathbf{C}_{2})}$$\end{document}

For the communication-subspace analyses (Figures 2g and 3k, l), source and target populations of 30 principal neurons were drawn at random from the 72 neurons of each area, and prediction performance and dimensionality were averaged over random draws. The dependence of the dimensionality on the number of modeled and sampled neurons is characterized in Appendix 1—figure 9.

sec.title: Interpretation of the results
sec.p: The prediction performance (Equation 22) is governed by the interplay between the source (C1\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{1}$\end{document}), target (C2\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{2}$\end{document}), and cross-population (C3\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{3}$\end{document}) covariances. The effectiveness of communication (indicated by a large predictive performance) can be understood through three key factors: (1) Source-target correlation: Prediction performance is directly enhanced by a stronger correlation between the source and target populations (i.e. larger C3\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{3}$\end{document} norm). (2) Signal reliability: Prediction performance is boosted by the reliability of the signals. Less noisy activity in source and target populations, indicated by smaller diagonal entries in C1\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{1}$\end{document} and C2\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{2}$\end{document}, leads to better prediction performance. (3) Alignment: Prediction performance is maximized when the principal directions of source covariance (eigenvectors of C1\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{1}$\end{document}) align with the principal directions of source-target covariance (left singular vectors of C3\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{3}$\end{document}).

This framework also explains the results in the frequency domain. The key metric here is the cross-power spectrum, which is the Fourier transform of the cross-covariances, and coherence, which is the squared cross-power spectrum normalized by the product of the auto-spectra, Equation 7. At frequencies of high coherence, i.e., of large cross-covariance between source and target relative to their auto-covariances, the prediction performance is necessarily highest as well, since both quantities are computed from the same cross-spectral density matrix.

The dimensionality of the communication subspace is given by the rank of the matrix C^2=C3TC1−1C3\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}=\mathbf{C}_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1}^{-1}\mathbf{C}_ {3}$\end{document}. Since the source covariance matrix C1\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{1}$\end{document} is a full-rank matrix, the dimensionality of the subspace is governed by the rank of the cross-covariance matrix, C3\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{3}$\end{document}. In the frequency domain, this means the dimensionality at a specific frequency is determined by the rank of the cross-power spectral density matrix (see Appendix 1—figure 5a). Our results show that the extent of normalization from surrounding neurons plays a critical role in shaping the dimensionality of the communication subspace. With surround normalization, dimensionality decreases specifically at frequencies where coherence is strongest (Figure 4c). Normalization reduces dimensionality because when just a small subset of neurons is strongly driven, and their responses are highly correlated across areas (V1 and V2), normalization suppresses the activity of surrounding neurons with weaker drive. This suppression, resembling a soft winner-take-all process, diminishes the contribution of those less active neurons to the population’s shared variability, leading to a lower effective dimensionality.
In contrast, without this normalization, no such correlation between coherence and dimensionality is observed (Appendix 1—figure 4h).

sec.title: Frequency decomposition of the communication subspace
sec.p: To analyze how communication between different brain areas varies across frequencies, we consider the frequency decomposition of the neural responses. The Wiener-Khinchin theorem states that the autocorrelation function C(τ)\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}(\tau)$\end{document} is the inverse Fourier transform of the power spectral density (PSD) matrix (S(ω)\begin{document}$\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)$\end{document}):(23)C(τ)=∫−∞∞S(ω)eıωτdω\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{C}(\tau)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)e^{\imath\omega \tau}d\omega$$\end{document}

To isolate C(τ)\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}(\tau)$\end{document} at a particular frequency (ω∗\begin{document}$\omega^{*}$\end{document}), we apply an idealized narrow band-pass filter centered at ω∗\begin{document}$\omega^{*}$\end{document}. Specifically, the filter’s transfer function H(ω)\begin{document}$H(\omega)$\end{document} is given by:(24)H(ω)={1if ω∈A0otherwise\begin{document}$$\displaystyle H(\omega) = \begin{cases}1 & \text{if } \omega \in A \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$\end{document}

where A=[ω∗−ϵ,ω∗+ϵ]∪[−ω∗−ϵ,−ω∗+ϵ]\begin{document}$A=[\omega^{*}-\epsilon,\omega^{*}+\epsilon]\cup[-\omega^{*}-\epsilon,-\omega^{ *}+\epsilon]$\end{document}, and ϵ\begin{document}$\epsilon$\end{document} is a small positive value defining the narrow bandwidth 2ϵ\begin{document}$2\epsilon$\end{document} around ω∗\begin{document}$\omega^{*}$\end{document}. The spectral density matrix of this filtered signal is given by:(25)Sfiltered(ω)=|H(ω)|2S(ω)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{\boldsymbol S}_{filtered}(\omega)=|H(\omega)|^{2}\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)$$\end{document}

The resulting autocorrelation of the filtered signal is expressed as:(26)Cfiltered(τ)=∫−∞∞Sfiltered(ω)eıωτdω=∫−∞∞|H(ω)|2S(ω)eıωτdω.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \begin{array}{ll}\mathbf{C}_{filtered}(\tau) & =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}{\boldsymbol S} _{filtered}(\omega)e^{\imath\omega\tau}d\omega\\ & =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|H(\omega)|^{2}{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)e^{\imath\omega \tau}d\omega.\end{array}$$\end{document}

Using the definition of H(ω)\begin{document}$H(\omega)$\end{document} and assuming ϵ\begin{document}$\epsilon$\end{document} to be sufficiently small such that S(ω)\begin{document}$\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)$\end{document} and eıωτ\begin{document}$e^{\imath\omega\tau}$\end{document} are approximately constant over the integration intervals of width 2ϵ\begin{document}$2\epsilon$\end{document}, the frequency-specific autocorrelation at ω∗\begin{document}$\omega^{*}$\end{document} is:(27)C(τ)|ω∗≈2ϵ(S(−ω∗)e−ıω∗τ+S(ω∗)eıω∗τ).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{C}(\tau)|_{\omega^{*}}\approx 2\epsilon\left(\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(-\omega^{*})e^{-\imath\omega^{*}\tau}+\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega^{*})e^{\imath\omega^{*}\tau} \right).$$\end{document}

At zero time lag (τ=0\begin{document}$\tau=0$\end{document}),(28)C(0)|ω∗≈2ϵ(S(−ω∗)+S(ω∗)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{C}(0)|_{\omega^{*}}\approx 2\epsilon\left(\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(-\omega^{*})+ \mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega^{*})\right).$$\end{document}

Since the PSD is Hermitian, i.e., S(ω)=S∗(−ω)\begin{document}$\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)=\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}^{*}(-\omega)$\end{document}, we have(29)C(0)|ω∗=4ϵRe{S(ω∗)}\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{C}(0)|_{\omega^{*}}=4\epsilon\,\text{Re}\{\mathcal{ \boldsymbol S}(\omega^{*})\}$$\end{document}

This frequency-specific autocorrelation matrix (C(0)|ω∗\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}(0)|_{\omega^{*}}$\end{document}) can then be used in place of C(0)\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}(0)$\end{document} in the communication subspace analysis described above to evaluate the prediction performance at any frequency. As our analysis does not depend on the absolute scaling of this matrix, the prefactor 4ϵ\begin{document}$4\epsilon$\end{document} can be disregarded, and we effectively use Re{S(ω∗)}\begin{document}$\text{Re}\{\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega^{*})\}$\end{document} as the frequency-specific correlation matrix.

sec.title: Application to experimental measurements
sec.p: The same construction applies directly to experimental recordings, and no band-pass filtering or separate regression per frequency band is required. Given simultaneously recorded source (e.g. V1) and target (e.g. V2) population activity (spike counts or LFP), one estimates the cross-spectral density matrix C(0)|ω∗=4ϵRe{S(ω∗)}\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}(0)|_{\omega^{*}}=4\epsilon\,\text{Re}\{\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega^{*})\}$\end{document} of the pooled population (e.g. by Welch’s or the multitaper method). At each frequency ω∗\begin{document}$\omega^{*}$\end{document}, Re{S(ω∗)}\begin{document}$\text{Re}\{\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega^{*})\}$\end{document} is the frequency-specific covariance matrix; partitioning it into the source, target, and cross blocks C1\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{1}$\end{document}, C2\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{2}$\end{document}, and C3\begin{document}$\mathbf{C}_{3}$\end{document} gives C^2=C3TC1−1C3\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}=\mathbf{C}_{3}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{C}_{1}^{-1}\mathbf{C}_ {3}$\end{document}, the prediction performance at each rank (Equation 20), and the dimensionality, i.e., the number of eigenvalues of C^2\begin{document}$\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{2}$\end{document} required to reach the full-rank performance (Equation 22) within a fixed tolerance. Repeating this at every frequency yields the experimental counterparts of Figure 4b and c. The prediction to be tested is that the dimensionality is smallest at the frequency of peak V1-V2 coherence and that this frequency increases with contrast.

sec.title: Numerical validation of the analytical spectra

caption.title: Validation of the analytical power and coherence spectra against direct stochastic simulation.
caption.p: The full nonlinear stochastic system (main text, Methods, ‘Power and coherence spectra’; noise model in ‘Intrinsic neural circuit noise’, and ‘Extrinsic noise in the LFP’ below) was integrated numerically, and the spectra were estimated directly from the simulated trajectories (light, jagged lines; stochastic differential equation [‘SDE’]) and compared with the closed-form expressions obtained by linearizing the dynamics about the fixed point (dark, smooth lines; ‘Analytical’). Line color indicates stimulus contrast (increasing from light to dark); all other parameters are the baseline values (Appendix 1—table 1). (a) Normalized V1 power spectra. (b) V1-V2 coherence spectra. Bottom panels show the residual (SDE – Analytical) at each contrast. Across all contrasts, the root-mean-square error (RMSE) is below 0.02 and the maximum absolute deviation is below 0.08 (power: RMSE < 0.017, max|SDE−Analytical|<0.071\begin{document}$\max|\mathrm{SDE}-\mathrm{Analytical}| \lt 0.071$\end{document}; coherence: RMSE < 0.018, max|SDE−Analytical|<0.072\begin{document}$\max|\mathrm{SDE}-\mathrm{Analytical}| \lt 0.072$\end{document}), confirming that the linearization is accurate in this parameter regime.

sec.p: The power and coherence spectra reported in the main text are obtained by linearizing the stochastic dynamics about the fixed point (main text, Methods, ‘Power and coherence spectra’). To verify this linearization, we integrated the full nonlinear stochastic system, i.e., the membrane-potential dynamics (Equations 60–67), the firing-rate dynamics with firing-rate noise (Equation 72), and the filtered synaptic noise (Equation 73), with the Euler-Maruyama scheme at the baseline parameters (Appendix 1—table 1) and noise parameters (Appendix 1—table 3). Trajectories were initialized at the deterministic fixed point and integrated with a time step of 10 µs (the fastest mode of the linearized system has a time constant of about 0.5 ms); after a burn-in of 1 s, 100 independent trials of 16 s were recorded at each contrast of the sweep shown in Figure 2c and e (0%, 2.5%, 3.7%, 6.1%, 9.7%, 16.3%, 35.9%, 50.3%, and 72%). Power spectra and cross-spectra of the membrane potentials were estimated by Welch’s method (segments of 4 s, 50% overlap) and averaged over trials; the extrinsic LFP noise (‘Extrinsic noise in the LFP’ below), which is independent of the circuit dynamics, was added analytically to the estimated spectra, exactly as in the analytical calculation. The simulated power spectra were normalized by the simulated spectrum at 0% contrast, with the same normalization as in the main text, and the coherence was computed between the maximally driven principal neurons in V1 and V2 (main text, Equation 7). The comparison with the closed-form expressions is shown in Appendix 1—figure 6: across all contrasts, the root-mean-square deviation is below 0.017 for the normalized power and below 0.018 for the coherence, and the maximum absolute deviation is below 0.072, confirming that the linearization is accurate at the baseline parameters. The linearization holds for small fluctuations about the fixed point, and the simulations bear this out. When the amplitudes of the noise sources are increased beyond the values of Appendix 1—table 3, the deviation between the simulated and the analytical spectra grows, and it does so first at the lowest contrasts (<10%): there the activities lie near zero, the noise fluctuations can drive them negative, and the rectification clips them to zero, which the linearized dynamics do not capture. Changing the absolute noise amplitude does not change the analytical results, since the plotted spectra are normalized. The deviations do not, however, grow with the gains: changing the input or feedback gain changes the fixed point, and the linearization about the new fixed point remains valid, because its accuracy is controlled by the strength of the fluctuations relative to the fixed point rather than by the gains themselves. All results reported in the paper use the baseline parameters, for which the linearization is accurate at every contrast and for all reported gain values; the stable ranges of the gains are given in Appendix 1—table 2.

sec.title: Quantitative fit to experimental power and coherence spectra

caption.title: Quantitative fit of the theory to experimental power and coherence spectra.
caption.p: Unlike Figure 2 of the main text, in which the theory is compared with data using a single, unfitted set of baseline parameters, here the model parameters were optimized to fit the experimental spectra measured in macaque V1 and V2 (Roberts et al., 2013). Dotted lines with circles: experiment; solid lines: model fit. Line color indicates stimulus contrast (%; legend). (a) Normalized V1 power spectra at six contrast levels (3.7%, 6.1%, 16.3%, 35.9%, 50.3%, and 72.0%). (b) V1-V2 coherence spectra at six contrast levels (3.7%, 9.7%, 16.3%, 35.9%, 50.3%, and 72.0%). Bottom panels show the residual (Experiment – Model) at each contrast. The fitted model captures the shift of the gamma peak toward higher frequencies with increasing contrast, the non-monotonic dependence of peak amplitude on contrast, and the high coherence at low frequencies for low contrasts.

sec.p: All comparisons between theory and experiment in the main text use a single, unfitted set of baseline parameters. To quantify how well the theory can account for experimentally measured spectra, we fit the model to the V1 power spectra and V1–V2 coherence spectra of Roberts et al., 2013 (digitized from the published figures at eight contrast levels: 2.5%, 3.7%, 6.1%, 9.7%, 16.3%, 35.9%, 50.3%, and 72%). The fitted model is the same circuit as in the main text, with the connectivity matrices (Wzx\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{zx}$\end{document}, W11\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{11}$\end{document}, W22\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{22}$\end{document}, W12=W21T\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{12}=\mathbf{W}_{21}^{\mathsf{T}}$\end{document}), the all-ones normalization pool, and the number of neurons per area held fixed. The free parameters were the gains, the time constants, the noise parameters, the semi-saturation constants σ1,2\begin{document}$\sigma_{1,2}$\end{document} and α1,2\begin{document}$\alpha_{1,2}$\end{document} (32 free parameters in total; Appendix 1—tables 1 and 3). The power and coherence spectra were fitted separately, giving two parameter sets. The objective, the MSE between the model and the experimental spectra over all contrasts and frequencies, was minimized with Adam on a bounded reparametrization of the parameters. Gradients were obtained by automatic differentiation through the fixed point (implicit differentiation), the linearization, and the spectra. The power fit used all eight contrasts with equal weight.

The fitted parameters remain close to the baseline set: γ1≈1.07\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}\approx 1.07$\end{document} and σ1≈0.077\begin{document}$\sigma_{1}\approx 0.077$\end{document} (baseline values 1.0 and 0.07), β1≈0.7\begin{document}$\beta_{1}\approx 0.7$\end{document}, β2≈1.2−1.4\begin{document}$\beta_{2}\approx 1.2-1.4$\end{document}, α1≈14−20\begin{document}$\alpha_{1}\approx 14-20$\end{document} (baseline 10), and all time constants between 0.2 and 3 ms. The resulting fits are shown in Appendix 1—figure 7: the root-mean-square deviation is below 0.062 for the normalized power and below 0.048 for the coherence at every contrast.

sec.title: Robustness with respect to model parameters
sec.p: All the results in this paper are obtained from the same set of parameters (Appendix 1—table 1) unless otherwise specified. To ensure the robustness of our findings, we verified them against a wide range of model parameters. We systematically repeated the calculations and simulations described above, varying each parameter individually while holding others at their baseline values. These parameter ranges are specified in Appendix 1—table 2. Overall, our key findings remain robust across a wide range of parameter regimes without requiring precise parameter tuning:

list-item.p: Contrast-response functions (Figure 2a). Higher cortical area (V2) consistently exhibits greater contrast gain, reflected by a lower semi-saturation contrast and a steeper exponent than lower cortical area (V1).
Gamma oscillations (Figure 2c and e). Both the power spectra and coherence spectra consistently exhibit prominent gamma-band peaks that shift to higher frequencies as contrast increases.
Alpha oscillations (Figure 3c). Low contrast inputs and weak feedback gain consistently produce clear alpha-band peaks in the power spectra.
Communication subspaces (Figure 2g). The V1-V2 subspace is consistently lower dimensional than the V1-V1 subspace.
Communication subspaces and feedback gain (Figure 3k). The V1-V2 communication strength consistently increases with increasing feedback gain.
Communication subspaces and V1 input gain (Figure 3l). V1-V1 and V1-V2 communication strength consistently decrease with increasing V1 input gain.

V2 input gain (Appendix 1—figure 8). Increasing the V2 input gain consistently enhances inter-areal (V1-V2) communication while leaving within-area (V1-V1) communication approximately unchanged, and shifts the gamma peaks in power and coherence to higher frequencies while broadening them and reducing their amplitude.

Frequency dependence of communication subspaces (Figure 4). The communication strength peaks consistently at the same frequencies as coherence for each contrast level, and subspace dimensionality is minimized at those frequencies.

Dynamic functional connectivity (Figure 5). Enhancing feedback from V4 to V1 consistently boosts communication between V1 and V4, and likewise, enhancing feedback from V5 to V1 selectively enhances communication between V1 and V5.

Dimensionality of inter-areal communication subspaces (Appendix 1—figure 4l and p). The dimensionality is consistently low when the input drive is localized (e.g. gratings). However, delocalized input drives (e.g. naturalistic images) result in a higher dimensionality. Fully all-to-all connections between V1 and V2 also produce a higher subspace dimensionality.

Oscillatory activity depends on normalization. Removing normalization consistently eliminates the gamma-band peaks in the power spectrum, coherence spectrum, and communication strength (Appendix 1—figure 4e, f, and g).
The dimensionality of the communication subspace is governed by the rank of the cross-covariance matrix, which itself depends crucially on normalization (Appendix 1—figure 5).

caption.p: This figure extends Figure 3 of the main text to include modulation of the V2 input gain (the gain of the V1 → V2 drive) on the same footing as feedback and V1 input gain. Line color intensity indicates the gain value (legends at top). Feedback gain was varied over γ1∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1}\begin{document}$\gamma_{1}\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\}$\end{document} and input gains over β1,2∈{0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5}\begin{document}$\beta_{1,2}\in\{0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5\}$\end{document}, with the other two gains held at their baseline values. In p–r, source and target populations of 30 neurons were drawn at random from the 72 principal neurons of each area, and the prediction performance was averaged over 200 random draws. (a–c) Firing rates as a function of contrast in V1 and V2. Increasing either feedback gain (a) or V1 input gain (b) enhances responses in both areas, whereas V2 input gain (c) leaves V1 responses unchanged and enhances only V2 responses. (d–f) V1 power spectra at 3% contrast. The alpha peak observed at low feedback gain (d) is absent when V1 input gain (e) or V2 input gain (f) is varied. (g–i) V1 power spectra at 50% contrast. The gamma peak shifts toward higher frequencies with increasing feedback gain (g), V1 input gain (h), and V2 input gain (i). Its bandwidth narrows with increasing V1 input gain but broadens with increasing feedback gain or V2 input gain, and its amplitude decreases with increasing V2 input gain. (j–l) V1–V2 coherence spectra at 3% contrast. A broad beta-band peak is observed only at low feedback gain (j); no such peak is observed for changes in V1 input gain (k) or V2 input gain (l). (m–o) V1–V2 coherence spectra at 50% contrast. The gamma coherence peak shifts toward higher frequencies with increasing feedback gain (m), V1 input gain (n), and V2 input gain (o); with increasing V2 input gain, the peak also broadens and its amplitude decreases. (p–r) Maximum prediction performance of inter-areal (V1–V2, circles) and within-area (V1–V1, squares) communication subspaces at 100% contrast, as a function of each gain. Increasing feedback gain enhances inter-areal communication while reducing within-area communication (p); increasing V1 input gain reduces both (q); increasing V2 input gain enhances inter-areal communication while leaving within-area communication approximately unchanged (r).

caption.p: Dimensionality of the inter-areal (V1–V2, circles) and within-area (V1–V1, squares) communication subspaces at 100% contrast and baseline parameters, defined as the smallest number of predictive dimensions at which the prediction performance reaches 95% of its full-rank value. Symbols show the mean, and shaded regions ±1 standard deviation, over 200 random draws of source and target populations. Left: The number of modeled principal neurons per area was varied (N=9\begin{document}$N=9$\end{document}, 18, 36, 72, and 144) while the sampled fraction was held at a fixed value (≈42%)\begin{document}$(\approx 42\%)$\end{document}. Right: The number of sampled source and target neurons was varied (5–30) at the value N=72\begin{document}$N=72$\end{document} used in the main text. Absolute dimensionality values therefore depend on the population size, and comparisons with experimental estimates should be made at matched population sizes, as in Figure 2g and h of the main text.

sec.title: Derivation of the general hierarchical recurrent normalization circuit
sec.p: This appendix provides a detailed derivation of the general dynamical equations for the hierarchical recurrent normalization model with reciprocal connections.

We begin with the primary visual cortex (V1). Assuming N1\begin{document}$\mathbf{N}_{1}$\end{document} is the normalization weight matrix for V1 and z1\begin{document}$\mathbf{z}_{1}$\end{document} is the input drive to V1, we can write the normalization equations for the V1 principal neurons with complementary receptive fields as:(30)y1s+=⌊z1⌋nσn+N1(⌊z1⌋n+⌊−z1⌋n)y1s−=⌊−z1⌋nσn+N1(⌊z1⌋n+⌊−z1⌋n)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{y}_1^{s+}=\frac{\lfloor\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n}}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n}+\mathbf {N}_{1}(\lfloor\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n}+\lfloor-\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n})} \qquad\qquad \mathbf{y}_1^{s-}=\frac{\lfloor-\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n}}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n}+\mathbf {N}_{1}(\lfloor\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n}+\lfloor-\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n})}$$\end{document}

where y1s+\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}^{s+}$\end{document} and y1s−\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}^{s-}$\end{document} represent the steady-state firing rates of principal neurons corresponding to positive (⌊z1⌋n\begin{document}$\lfloor\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n}$\end{document}) and negative ⌊−z1⌋n\begin{document}$\lfloor-\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n}$\end{document} input drives, respectively. Here, σ\begin{document}$\sigma$\end{document} represents the semi-saturation constant. The exponent n\begin{document}$n$\end{document} is typically observed to be n≈2\begin{document}$n\approx 2$\end{document} for the primary visual cortex; it can be different for different brain areas. Mathematically:(31)⌊z1⌋n+⌊−z1⌋n=|z1|n\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \lfloor\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n} + \lfloor-\mathbf{z}_{1}\rfloor^{n} = \left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n}$$\end{document}

Our goal is to derive the dynamical equations for a general n\begin{document}$n$\end{document}, which yield the fixed points defined by Equation 30. First, we distinguish between the membrane potentials and the firing rates of neurons. The membrane potential of a given type of neuron is denoted by vectors such as y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}, u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document}, a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}, and q1\begin{document}$\mathbf{q}_{1}$\end{document}. Their corresponding firing rates are y1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}^{+}$\end{document} (and y1−\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}^{-}$\end{document} for complementary responses), u1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+}$\end{document}, a1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}^{+}$\end{document}, and q1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{q}_{1}^{+}$\end{document}. The instantaneous firing rates are related to membrane potentials by applying rectification (denoted by ⌊⋅⌋\begin{document}$\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$\end{document}) followed by power-law activation (Heeger, 1992a),(32)x+=⌊x⌋β.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{x}^{+} = \lfloor\mathbf{x}\rfloor^{\beta}.$$\end{document}

The values of β\begin{document}$\beta$\end{document} are taken to be {2,12\begin{document}$\frac{1}{2}$\end{document},1,1} for {y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}, u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document}, a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}, q1\begin{document}$\mathbf{q}_{1}$\end{document}}, respectively. Combining the firing rates of principal neurons with the complementary receptive fields, y1s+\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}^{s+}$\end{document} and y1s−\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}^{s-}$\end{document}, Equation 30 can be alternatively written as:(33)|y1|n=y1s++y1s−=|z1|nσn+N1|z1|n\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n} = \mathbf{y}_{1}^{s+}+ \mathbf{y}_{1}^{s-}= \frac{\left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n}}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} + \mathbf{N}_{1}\left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n}}$$\end{document}

To proceed with our derivation, we need to isolate the |z1|n\begin{document}$\left|\mathbf{z}_{1}\right|^{n}$\end{document} term. From Equation 33, we have:(34)|z1|n=σn⊙|y1|n+|y1|n⊙(N1|z1|n)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n}&= \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n} + \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n} \odot (\mathbf{N}_{1}\left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n}) $$\end{document}

where ⊙\begin{document}$\odot$\end{document} denotes element-wise multiplication. Using the identity x1⊙x2=D(x1)x2\begin{document}$\mathbf{x}_{1}\odot\mathbf{x}_{2}=\mathrm{D}(\mathbf{x}_{1})\mathbf{x}_{2}$\end{document}, where D(x1)\begin{document}$\mathrm{D}(\mathbf{x}_{1})$\end{document} is a diagonal matrix with the elements of vector x1\begin{document}$\mathbf{x}_{1}$\end{document} on its diagonal, we can rewrite and solve for |z1|n\begin{document}$\left|\mathbf{z}_{1}\right|^{n}$\end{document}:(35)|z1|n=σn⊙|y1|n+D(|y1|n)N1|z1|n\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n} + \mathrm{D}(\left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})\mathbf{N}_{1}\left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n}$$\end{document}

Factoring out |z1|n\begin{document}$\left|\mathbf{z}_{1}\right|^{n}$\end{document}:(36)[I−D(|y1|n)N1]|z1|n=σn⊙|y1|n\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left [\mathbf{I}- \mathrm{D}\left (\left|\mathbf{y}_{1}\right|^{n}\right)\mathbf{N}_{1}\right] \left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}$$\end{document}

Multiplying both sides with [I−D(|y1|n)N1]−1\begin{document}$[\mathbf{I}-\mathrm{D}(\left|\mathbf{y}_{1}\right|^{n})\mathbf{N}_{1}]^{-1}$\end{document} from the left yields:(37)|z1|n=[I−D(|y1|n)N1]−1(σn⊙|y1|n)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n} = \left [\mathbf{I}- \mathrm{D}(\left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})\mathbf{N}_{1}\right ]^{-1}\left (\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}\right) $$\end{document}

This expression for |z1|n\begin{document}$\left|\mathbf{z}_{1}\right|^{n}$\end{document} will be used in subsequent steps. Now, we introduce the dynamical equation for the membrane potential y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document} of the principal V1 neurons, consistent with biological computation in pyramidal cells (see main text, ‘Biological plausibility’):(38)τy1dy1dt=−y1+b1⊙z1+11+a1+⊙(W11((y1+)1n−(y1−)1n)+γ1⊙W12(y2+)1n).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{y_1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}= -\mathbf{y}_{1} + \mathbf{b}_{1} \odot \mathbf{z}_{1} + \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot \left(\mathbf{W}_{11}\left(({\mathbf{y}_1^+})^{\frac{1}{n}}- ({\mathbf{y}_1^-})^{\frac{1}{n}}\right) + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}({\mathbf{y}_2^+})^{\frac{1}{n}}\right).$$\end{document}

Here, τy1\begin{document}$\tau_{y_{1}}$\end{document} is the time constant, b1\begin{document}$\mathbf{b}_{1}$\end{document} is the input gain, a1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}^{+}$\end{document} represents firing rates of the inhibitory neuron population. W11\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{11}$\end{document} is the recurrent V1 connectivity matrix, W12\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{12}$\end{document} is the connectivity matrix containing the synaptic weights from V2 to V1. W12(y2+)1n\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{12}({\mathbf{y}_{2}^{+}})^{\frac{1}{n}}$\end{document} represents the feedback signal from V2 to V1, calculated as the weighted sum of the activities of V2 neurons. γ1 is the feedback gain modulation parameter. y2+\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{2}^{+}$\end{document} is the firing rate of V2 principal neurons, defined as ⌊y2⌋n\begin{document}$\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor^{n}$\end{document}.

For simplicity, we assume that the recurrent weight matrix W11=I\begin{document}$\mathbf{W}_{11}=\mathrm{I}$\end{document}. Given that (y1+)1/n−(y1−)1/n=⌊y1⌋−⌊−y1⌋=y1\begin{document}$(\mathbf{y}_{1}^{+})^{1/n}-(\mathbf{y}_{1}^{-})^{1/n}=\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{1} \rfloor-\lfloor-\mathbf{y}_{1}\rfloor=\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document} and (y2+)1/n=⌊y2⌋\begin{document}$({\mathbf{y}_{2}^{+}})^{1/n}=\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor$\end{document}, the equation for y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document} simplifies to:(39)τy1dy1dt=−y1+b1⊙z1+11+a1+⊙(y1+γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{y_1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}= -\mathbf{y}_{1} + \mathbf{b}_{1} \odot \mathbf{z}_{1} + \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot \left(\mathbf{y}_{1} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor \right)$$\end{document}

Now at steady state, dy1dt=0\begin{document}$\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}=0$\end{document},(40)0=−y1+b1⊙z1+11+a1+⊙(y1+γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle 0 = -\mathbf{y}_{1} + \mathbf{b}_{1} \odot \mathbf{z}_{1} + \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot \left(\mathbf{y}_{1} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor \right)$$\end{document}

Expanding the terms:(41)0=−y1+b1⊙z1+11+a1+⊙y1+11+a1+⊙(γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle 0 = -\mathbf{y}_{1} + \mathbf{b}_{1} \odot \mathbf{z}_{1} + \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot \mathbf{y}_{1} + \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot (\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor)$$\end{document}

Rearranging terms:(42)a1+1+a1+⊙y1=b1⊙z1+11+a1+⊙(γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{\mathbf{a}_1^{+}}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot \mathbf{y}_{1} = \mathbf{b}_{1} \odot \mathbf{z}_{1} + \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot (\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor)$$\end{document}

Moving the feedback term to the left-hand side:(43)a1+1+a1+⊙y1−11+a1+⊙(γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋)=b1⊙z1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{\mathbf{a}_1^{+}}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot \mathbf{y}_{1} - \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot (\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor) = \mathbf{b}_{1} \odot \mathbf{z}_{1}$$\end{document}

Factoring out y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}:(44)y1⊙(a1+1+a1+−11+a1+⊙γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋y1)=b1⊙z1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{y}_{1} \odot \left(\frac{\mathbf{a}_1^{+}}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}- \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot \frac{\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor}{\mathbf{y}_{1}}\right) = \mathbf{b}_{1} \odot \mathbf{z}_{1}$$\end{document}

We define a modulatory term u1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+}$\end{document}, such that:(45)y1⊙u1+=b1⊙z1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{y}_{1} \odot \mathbf{u}_{1}^{+} = \mathbf{b}_{1} \odot \mathbf{z}_{1} $$\end{document}

where(46)u1+=a1+1+a1+−11+a1+⊙γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋y1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{u}_{1}^{+} = \frac{\mathbf{a}_1^{+}}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}- \frac{1}{1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}}\odot \frac{\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor}{\mathbf{y}_{1}}$$\end{document}

Next, we derive the dynamical equation for a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}, from the definition of u1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+}$\end{document}:(47)u1+⊙(1+a1+)=a1+−γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋y1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{u}_{1}^{+} \odot (1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}) = \mathbf{a}_1^{+} - \frac{\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor}{\mathbf{y}_{1}}$$\end{document}

Upon rearranging,(48)0=−a1++γ1⊙W12⌊y2⌋y1+(1+a1+)⊙u1+\begin{document}$$\displaystyle 0 = -\mathbf{a}_1^{+} + \frac{\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor}{\mathbf{y}_{1}}+ (1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}) \odot \mathbf{u}_{1}^{+}$$\end{document}

This equation describes the steady state of a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}. It exhibits a form analogous to that of y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}, comprising an input drive and a recurrent drive term. Therefore, we propose the following dynamical equation for the membrane potential a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}:(49)τa1⁢d⁢𝐚1d⁢t=-𝐚1+𝜸1⊙𝐖12⁢⌊𝐲2⌋𝐲1+(1+𝐚1+)⊙𝐮1+\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{a_{1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{a}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\mathbf{a}_{1}+\frac {\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1}\odot\mathbf{W}_{12}\lfloor\mathbf{y}_{2}\rfloor}{\mathbf{y}_{ 1}}+(1+\mathbf{a}_{1}^{+})\odot\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+}$$\end{document}

According to Dale’s law, the principal neurons y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}, which we hypothesize to be excitatory (main text, ‘Biological plausibility’), cannot directly inhibit other neurons. Therefore, the division by y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document} implies the existence of an intermediate inhibitory interneuron. We introduce an inhibitory interneuron population q1\begin{document}$\mathbf{q}_{1}$\end{document}, which tracks y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}:(50)τq1dq1dt=−q1+(y1+)1/n\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{q_1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{q}_1}{\mathrm{d}t}= -\mathbf{q}_1 + (\mathbf{y}^{+}_{1})^{1/n}$$\end{document}

With this interneuron, the dynamic equation for a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document} becomes:(51)τa1da1dt=−a1+γ1⊙W12(y2+)1/nq1++(1+a1+)⊙u1+\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{a_1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{a}_1}{\mathrm{d}t}= -\mathbf{a}_1 + \frac{\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1} \odot \mathbf{W}_{12}(\mathbf{y}_{2}^{+})^{1/n}}{\mathbf{q}_1^{+}}+ (1 + \mathbf{a}_1^{+}) \odot \mathbf{u}_{1}^{+}$$\end{document}

Now, we return to Equation 45 to derive the dynamical equation for the modulatory neuron u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document}. Starting with y1⊙u1+=b1⊙z1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}\odot\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+}=\mathbf{b}_{1}\odot\mathbf{z}_{1}$\end{document}, we take the modulus on both sides and raise to the power of n:(52)|y1|n⊙(u1+)n=b1n⊙|z1|n\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n} \odot (\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} = \mathbf{b}_{1}^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{z}_{1}\right |^{n}$$\end{document}

Substituting the expression for |z1|n\begin{document}$\left|\mathbf{z}_{1}\right|^{n}$\end{document} from Equation 37:(53)|y1|n⊙(u1+)n=b1n⊙[I−D(|y1|n)N1]−1(σn⊙|y1|n)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n} \odot (\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} = \mathbf{b}_{1}^{n} \odot [\mathbf{I}- \mathrm{D}(\left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})\mathbf{N}_{1}]^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})$$\end{document}

We assume that b1\begin{document}$\mathbf{b}_{1}$\end{document} has equal components, i.e., b1=b11\begin{document}$\mathbf{b}_{1}=b_{1}\mathbf{1}$\end{document}. Multiplying both sides by [I−D(|y1|n)N1]\begin{document}$[\mathbf{I}-\mathrm{D}(\left|\mathbf{y}_{1}\right|^{n})\mathbf{N}_{1}]$\end{document} and rearranging:(54)[I−D(|y1|n)N1]((u1+)n⊙|y1|nb1n)=σn⊙|y1|n\begin{document}$$\displaystyle [\mathbf{I}- \mathrm{D}(\left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})\mathbf{N}_{1}] \left(\frac{(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}}{\mathbf{b}_{1}^{n}}\right) = \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}$$\end{document}

Multiplying both sides by D(1|y1|n)\begin{document}$\mathrm{D}\left(\frac{1}{\left|\mathbf{y}_{1}\right|^{n}}\right)$\end{document}:(55)D(1|y1|n)[I−D(|y1|n)N1]((u1+)n⊙|y1|nb1n)=D(1|y1|n)(σn⊙|y1|n)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathrm{D}\left(\frac{1}{\left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}}\right) [\mathbf{I}- \mathrm{D}(\left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})\mathbf{N}_{1}] \left(\frac{(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}}{\mathbf{b}_{1}^{n}}\right) = \mathrm{D}\left(\frac{1}{\left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}}\right) (\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})$$\end{document}

This simplifies to:(56)(u1+)nb1n−N1((u1+)n⊙|y1|nb1n)=σn\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n}}{\mathbf{b}_{1}^{n}}- \mathbf{N}_{1} \left(\frac{(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}}{\mathbf{b}_{1}^{n}}\right) = \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n}$$\end{document}

Since we assumed that b1\begin{document}$\mathbf{b}_{1}$\end{document} has equal components, we get:(57)(u1+)n−N1((u1+)n⊙|y1|n)=σn⊙b1n\begin{document}$$\displaystyle (\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} - \mathbf{N}_{1} ((\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n}) = \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} \odot \mathbf{b}_{1}^{n}$$\end{document}

Elementwise multiplying both sides by u1/(u1+)n\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}/(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n}$\end{document} from left and rearrange:(58)0=−u1+u1(u1+)n⊙(b1n⊙σn+N1((u1+)n⊙|y1|n))\begin{document}$$\displaystyle 0 = -\mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\mathbf{u}_{1}}{(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n}}\odot \left(\mathbf{b}_{1}^{n} \odot \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} + \mathbf{N}_{1}((\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})\right)$$\end{document}

This equation describes the steady state of u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document}. We propose the following dynamical equation for u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document},(59)τu1du1dt=−u1+u1(u1+)n⊙(b1n⊙σn+N1((u1+)n⊙|y1|n))\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{u_1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{u}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}= -\mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\mathbf{u}_{1}}{(\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n}}\odot \left(\mathbf{b}_{1}^{n} \odot \boldsymbol{\sigma}^{n} + \mathbf{N}_{1}((\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+})^{n} \odot \left |\mathbf{y}_{1}\right |^{n})\right)$$\end{document}

Equations 39, 50, 51, and 59 describe the dynamics of principal neurons, modulatory inhibitory neurons, and modulatory excitatory neurons in V1. They exhibit the fixed point solution given by the normalization by design. These equations are general for any choice of n\begin{document}$n$\end{document} and β\begin{document}$\beta$\end{document}. We get a particularly simplified form when we set n=2\begin{document}$n=2$\end{document} and β={2,12,1,1}\begin{document}$\beta=\{2,\frac{1}{2},1,1\}$\end{document} for {y1\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}$\end{document}, u1\begin{document}$\mathbf{u}_{1}$\end{document}, a1\begin{document}$\mathbf{a}_{1}$\end{document}, q1\begin{document}$\mathbf{q}_{1}$\end{document}}, respectively.

sec.title: Intrinsic neural circuit noise
sec.p: The influence of noise on the deterministic neural dynamics is treated analytically in this model. We consider two primary sources of noise: firing rate noise originating from the spiking process and synaptic noise.

Firing rate noise is added to the firing rate vector k+\begin{document}$\mathbf{k}^{+}$\end{document}, where k+\begin{document}$\mathbf{k}^{+}$\end{document} represents various neural population firing rates (e.g. excitatory like y1+,u1+or inhibitory likea1+,q1+\begin{document}$\mathbf{y}_{1}^{+},\mathbf{u}_{1}^{+}\text{or inhibitory like}\ \mathbf{a}_{1} ^{+},\mathbf{q}_{1}^{+}$\end{document}). This noise is attributed to the spiking mechanism, whose strength is found by the modified GR model (Rawat, 2025; Carandini, 2004). Due to the high degree of redundancy in neural circuits, the strength of this noise is quenched due to the averaging of these redundant signals. The result is that the noise has a negligible impact on the firing rate dynamics (Allen and Stevens, 1994; Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995). For a given firing rate vector k+\begin{document}$\mathbf{k}^{+}$\end{document}, with an associated activation exponent β\begin{document}$\beta$\end{document}, the noise dynamics are described by:(72)τk+dk+dt=−k++⌊k⌋β+σk⋅η(t),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{k^+}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{k}^{+}}{\mathrm{d}t}= -\mathbf{k}^{+} + \lfloor \mathbf{k}\rfloor^{\beta}+ \sigma_{k}\cdot \boldsymbol{\eta}(t), $$\end{document}

where τk+\begin{document}$\tau_{k^{+}}$\end{document} is the time constant for the firing rate dynamics of population k+\begin{document}$\mathbf{k}^{+}$\end{document}, σk\begin{document}$\sigma_{k}$\end{document} represents the noise strengths for different neuron types, and η(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{\eta}(t)$\end{document} is a vector of independent Gaussian white noise processes, each with zero mean and unit variance.

Synaptic noise is modeled as exponentially low-pass filtered Gaussian white noise (f\begin{document}$\mathbf{f}$\end{document}), given by the following SDE:(73)τf⁢d⁢𝐟d⁢t=-𝐟+σf⋅𝜼⁢(t),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{f}\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\mathbf{f}+ \sigma_{f}\cdot\boldsymbol{\eta}(t),$$\end{document}

where τf\begin{document}$\tau_{f}$\end{document} is the noise filtering time constant (τf=1\begin{document}$\tau_{f}=1$\end{document} ms, approximating the time constant of synaptic transmission), and σf\begin{document}$\sigma_{f}$\end{document} represents the noise strength. This filtered noise (f\begin{document}$\mathbf{f}$\end{document}) is then added to the dynamical equations for the membrane potentials of each neuron, Equations 60–67, and it is the main source of intrinsic noise.
Upon incorporating these sources of noise, we get a high-dimensional nonlinear stochastic dynamical system with the following variables:

list-item.p: Variables representing the membrane potential for different neuron types implementing normalization (Equations 60–67).
Firing rates (Equation 72) for each membrane potential variable.
Filtered synaptic noise (Equation 73) for each membrane potential variable.

sec.p: We then linearize this dynamical system about the fixed point found by simulating the deterministic part of the dynamical system, which gives us the Jacobian matrix J\begin{document}$\mathbf{J}$\end{document}. We also construct the dispersion matrix L\begin{document}$\mathbf{L}$\end{document} and the diffusion matrix D\begin{document}$\mathbf{D}$\end{document} using the strength of the noise added in various dynamical variables. The definition of these matrices allows us to compute the covariance matrix and power spectra analytically as discussed in the Methods section of the main text.

sec.title: Extrinsic noise in the LFP
sec.p: In addition to the noise sources detailed above, we also account for additional sources of noise that contribute to LFP power and coherence spectra. We consider two components of extrinsic noise: (1) Correlated noise (ζcorrelated\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{\mathrm{correlated}}$\end{document}), assumed to stem from the volume conduction of electric fields generated by transmembrane current through the extracellular brain tissue, with negligible impact on spiking activity and firing rates (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Bédard et al., 2006; Einevoll et al., 2013). (2) Uncorrelated noise (𝜻uncorrelated\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{\mathrm{uncorrelated}}$\end{document}), which encompasses noise from various other sources, including motion artifact, instrumentation noise, thermal noise, and biological sources of noise (Nelson and Pouget, 2010; Ludwig et al., 2009; Whitmore and Lin, 2016).

This extrinsic noise is added to the simulated neural responses (membrane potentials for different neuron types, denoted collectively by x\begin{document}$\mathbf{x}$\end{document}):(74)x′(t)=x(t)+ζuncorrelated(t)+ζcorrelated(t)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{x}(t) + \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{\mathrm{uncorrelated}}(t) + \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{\mathrm{correlated}}(t)$$\end{document}

Since these noise sources are uncorrelated with the responses of the neurons, the power spectrum of the measured signals S′(ω)\begin{document}$\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}^{\prime}(\omega)$\end{document} is the sum of the spectrum of the neurons’ activity S(ω)\begin{document}$\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)$\end{document} and the spectra of these noise components:(75)S′(ω)=S(ω)+Suncorrelated(ω)+Scorrelated(ω)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{\boldsymbol S}^{\prime}(\omega)=\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}(\omega)+\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}_{\mathrm{ uncorrelated}}(\omega)+\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}_{\mathrm{correlated}}(\omega)$$\end{document}

The correlated noise is modeled to produce a 1ω4\begin{document}$\frac{1}{\omega^{4}}$\end{document} power law scaling, which is achieved by doubly low-pass filtered white noise. Its power spectrum for each element is given by:(76)Scorrelated, element(ω)=Σcorr(1+τnoise2ω2)2\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{\boldsymbol S}_{\text{correlated, element}}(\omega)=\frac{\Sigma_{\mathrm{corr} }}{\left(1+\tau_{\text{noise}}^{2}\omega^{2}\right)^{2}}$$\end{document}

The uncorrelated power spectrum Suncorrelated(ω)\begin{document}$\mathcal{\boldsymbol S}_{\mathrm{uncorrelated}}(\omega)$\end{document} is diagonal, with each diagonal term having a similar filtered form:(77)Suncorrelated(ω)=D(Σuncorr(1+τnoise2ω2)2)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{\boldsymbol S}_{\text{uncorrelated}}(\omega)=\mathrm{D}\left(\frac{\Sigma_{ \mathrm{uncorr}}}{\left(1+\tau_{\text{noise}}^{2}\omega^{2}\right)^{2}}\right)$$\end{document}

In our simulation, the ratio of power spectral densities of the correlated noise to the uncorrelated noise (i.e. Σcorr/Σuncorr\begin{document}$\Sigma_{\mathrm{corr}}/{\Sigma_{\mathrm{uncorr}}}$\end{document} for corresponding element) is set to 10 for all the results. The noise parameters used in the simulation are given in Appendix 1—table 3.

body.p: This important study extends a model of cortical normalization (ORGaNICs) to interacting cortical areas and shows that communication through coherence and communication subspaces can arise from a single set of dynamics. The evidence is convincing, showing analytically that contrast-dependent gamma dynamics and a low-dimensional inter-areal communication subspace arise from one parameter set. The work will interest neuroscientists and theorists concerned with inter-areal communication, cortical oscillations, and divisive normalization.

[Editors' note: this version has been assessed by the Reviewing Editor without further input from the original reviewers. The authors have addressed the comments raised in the previous round of review.]

In this paper, Pal and colleagues propose a mechanistic unification of two influential accounts of inter-areal communication: communication through coherence and communication subspaces. A major strength of the paper is that it does not treat coherence and communication subspaces as independent phenomena, as typically done, but instead derives both from the same circuit with divisive normalization. In this framework, noise-driven fluctuations around the normalized fixed point determine covariance and cross-power structure (which, in retrospect, makes so much sense to be related). Then, they show how these determine linear prediction performance and the effective dimensionality of the communication subspace. They also show (however not very visually, see recommendation below for a figure) how divisive normalization is crucial to shape inter-areal coherence and the dimensionality of communication.

I found this conceptual contribution potentially very influential, but somewhat obscured by the technical complexity of the model. The central intuition (I think) is that recurrent normalization can organize cross-area fluctuations, both frequency-specific correlations and cross-covariances. Took me a while to grasp this insight, mostly because I was stuck with the model details. Note that I have some experience with network dynamics, but not with this particular model.
Summary:

The authors extend the ORGaNICs framework (a recurrent circuit that dynamically implements divisive normalization) to connected cortical areas with explicit top-down feedback. Because the network has a known analytical fixed point that coincides with (or closely approximates) the normalization equation, the authors can linearize about that fixed point and derive closed-form expressions for the power spectral density, inter-areal coherence, and communication subspaces. Using a two-area instantiation (V1 & V2) with a single fixed parameter set and no data fitting, they show the model reproduces: (i) contrast-response functions with steeper slope V2; (ii) gamma-band power and coherence peaks that shift to higher frequency with contrast; and (iii) a low-dimensional inter-areal communication subspace that is lower-dimensional than the within-area subspace. They derive parallel predictions of what happens by changing model parameters: feedback gain enhances inter-areal and suppresses within-area communication, and normalization is necessary for both the oscillatory dynamics and the reduced subspace dimensionality. A three-area extension (V1&V4, V1&V5/MT) is used to argue that differential top-down feedback can dynamically route functional connectivity.
Strengths:
(1) Analytical tractability: Deriving power spectra, coherence, and communication-subspace structure in closed form from a known fixed point is genuinely valuable.
(2) Conceptual unification: Framing coherence and communication subspaces as arising from the same normalization-driven dynamics is an elegant and useful contribution.
(3) Breadth from few assumptions: A large range of phenomena (contrast gain, gamma dynamics) emerges from normalization-based model assumptions.
(4) Biological grounding: The mapping of model variables onto identified cell types connects the abstract computation to known cortical microcircuitry.
(5) The prediction that input-gain versus feedback-gain modulation produce distinct spectral signatures gives experimentalists a clear way to test the framework.
Summary

The work of Pal and colleagues considers a hierarchical and multi-population version of the "oscillatory recurrent gated neural integrator circuits" (ORGaNICs) model, showing through analytics that the model captures multiple relevant experimental results: first of all, its oscillatory dynamics produce a profile with high resemblance to experimental results, both in terms of decay of power at high frequency and in terms of shifting peak as a function of stimulus contrast. Second, inter-areal communication subspace dimensionality is lower than within-area dimensionality. The authors then proceed to further characterize the model's response properties as a function of input and feedback gain. In particular, they find that frequencies transmitted with higher strength also carry more information, that changing gain modifies the dimensionality of communication subspaces, and that these properties can be used in a three-layer model, where an upstream area can select which downstream area to communicate to, based on the strength of feedback gain.
Strengths

This work demonstrates that a single-circuit model with normalization properties can capture both the oscillatory dynamics and the inter-areal communication properties measured in cortical circuits, matching multiple experimental results. The full analytical tractability of the model is highly advantageous, allowing for easier exploration of parameters, replicability, and effective interpretations of results compared to purely numerical approaches.

The work also makes a useful conceptual link between normalization, coherence-based communication, and subspace-based communication. In particular, it shows how both phenomena can emerge from the same circuit dynamics, where normalization is a key factor.

Interestingly, the model is also extended to multiple areas, showing how attention (in the form of changes in feedback gain) can synchronize the activity of a downstream area with one of two upstream areas, thus effectively selecting which area to communicate with.

In general, this is an interesting computational framework and a useful starting point for future modeling work. A particular strength is that it connects normalization, oscillatory dynamics, coherence, and communication subspaces within one analytically tractable model, making it possible to generate mechanistic hypotheses about when inter-areal communication should be stronger, lower-dimensional, or preferentially routed through feedback.
